findings.title: pipe-write completion reported OK although the supervisor never read the key; the declared premature-termination arm was unreachable
findings.mechanism_confirmed: The governed key frame is 92 bytes and the inherited anonymous descriptor is an ordinary kernel pipe with a 64 KiB buffer, so writer.write(frame, cb) always completes into the buffer and writer.end()'s callback resolved the settle promise within microseconds — long before the 250 ms timer that the 'exit'/'close' arm armed. Because done() was guarded by a `settled` flag, the premature arm's later done({ code: TRANSFER_WRITE_FAILED }) was a no-op, so that documented outcome was NOT REACHABLE AT ALL. The launcher returned ok:true with supervisor_pid set to a process that had already exited without ever reading fd 3.
findings.security_impact_assessment: Key containment was NOT breached — the authority was already TRANSFERRED_SPENT, the private key already deleted, buffers zeroed, retry refused, and the unread frame died with the pipe. The defect was EVIDENCE TRUTHFULNESS and LIVENESS: the launcher recorded a completed transfer and a live supervisor for a supervisor that provably never received the key. This Builder accepts the Checker's severity assessment and did not downgrade it.
correction: the unreachable 250 ms premature-termination timer is REMOVED — no timing heuristic is the authority decision anywhere on this path
write completion is no longer success: it only means the frame entered the pipe buffer, and the code and comments now say exactly that
new awaitVerifiedSupervisorClaim: a bounded, EXIT-DRIVEN wait for the ephemeral-SIGNED supervisor claim, which is the one acknowledgment a supervisor cannot fabricate

verifying that claim proves, in one artifact, that the exact spawned process (1) read and decoded the inherited key frame, (2) matched the ephemeral key to the consumed marker, (3) independently reverified the signed V4 activation, (4) proved its entrypoint identity, (5) minted a valid signed claim, and (6) bound it to the spawned PID and OS-observed start identity
the parent independently observes the child's OS start identity and compares it with the claim's, rather than trusting the claim against itself
a torn read of a half-written record is retried; a COMPLETE record that fails any binding is refused immediately, because claims are wx-once and can never become valid later
SUPERVISOR_CLAIM_WAIT_MS is a fixed module constant — no caller-configurable claim path, clock, timeout or verification bypass was introduced
the production launcher names the failure honestly: final_state SUPERVISOR_NEVER_ACKNOWLEDGED with stage supervisor_acknowledgment, distinct from a spawn failure

the test-support key-receipt child is now a GENUINE minimal supervisor (re-verifies, attaches, mints the claim) rather than a byte counter, because a byte counter is — correctly — no longer accepted as evidence of delivery
not_accepted_as_proof: the existence of a child PID
the child remaining alive for an arbitrary number of milliseconds

findings.title: stale FG_SPAWN_LOG comments contradicted the recording stub's actual mechanism — the exact class FG-FCHK-197-E was raised to fix
findings.mechanism_confirmed: The stub's header said it appends to 'the log named by FG_SPAWN_LOG' and the C1 comment said 'every process in the attack is given FG_SPAWN_LOG'. Neither was true: FG_SPAWN_LOG appeared nowhere in the repository except those two comments — no code set it and no code read it. The stub derives its log from import.meta.url, and lines 7-10 of the same file explicitly warn that an env-carried path would be scrubbed away by the production boundary. The two comments asserted precisely the mechanism the file warns against. The MEASUREMENT was correct; only the prose was wrong.

findings.title: deepFreezeAuthority silently dropped an own __proto__ data key and mutated the copy's prototype instead of refusing it
findings.mechanism_confirmed: `out` was created as {}, so it inherited Object.prototype's __proto__ ACCESSOR. When k === '__proto__', `out[k] = value` invoked that SETTER and reassigned the copy's prototype rather than creating an own data property. JSON.parse produces exactly this shape — an own, enumerable, writable __proto__ data property — so the one input class the module is built to consume could carry a key it neither refused nor copied faithfully. Observed before correction: no throw; the __proto__ key vanished from the copy; the prototype became the attacker's object; f.max_budget_usd resolved to 777777 by prototype-chain lookup; Object.isFrozen(f) and mutableAuthorityPaths(f) both still reported the copy as sound; and the module REFUSED its own output on round-trip with AUTHORITY_NON_PLAIN_PROTOTYPE — a self-inconsistency proving the copy was not the plain JSON authority data the contract promises.
findings.reachability_confirmed: NOT exploitable in production, and this Builder verified rather than assumed it. All three call sites (activation-v4.mjs makeCapability, and the CONSUMED and SUPERVISOR_EXECUTION mints in lifecycle-authority-v4.mjs) pass object literals whose key sets are hard-coded in source, and cap.limits / cap.exclusions are built by Object.fromEntries over the fixed V4_SIGNED_LIMIT_FIELDS and V4_SIGNED_EXCLUSIONS tables. No attacker-controlled key reaches the helper on any route. This was a latent contract gap in an explicitly-audited helper, not an authority escape.
correction: own keys named __proto__, constructor or prototype are REFUSED with the new AUTHORITY_DANGEROUS_KEY code
the rejection is recursive — it applies at every depth, including inside arrays
the copy is built with Object.create(null) and Object.defineProperty, never with property assignment, so no inherited setter can ever be invoked

the standard prototype is restored only AFTER every key has been materialised as an own data property, preserving the ordinary plain-object behaviour consumers require (JSON.stringify, Object.keys, spread, `in`, property reads)
the caller-owned source is still neither mutated nor frozen, and the previously-rejecting classes (unusual prototypes, accessors, symbols, functions, cycles, undefined/NaN/Infinity) still reject
